strengths: Well-motivated problem: Few-Patch Bias is clearly demonstrated through attention visualizations, masking experiments (18.7% ± 4.1% accuracy drop), and rigorous causal analysis using Total Direct Effect (TDE), with empirical evidence that uniform TDE distribution correlates with better generalization

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two settings and three datasets (GenImage, DRCT, Chameleon) with thorough robustness studies (JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, random masking), ablations, and strong quantitative results (97.2% GenImage, 99.50% DRCT, 72.07% Chameleon)

Exceptional stability improvements: significantly lower standard deviations than competing methods (1.7% vs 5.6% on GenImage; 0.1% vs 4.7% on DRCT), demonstrating practical robustness across diverse generative models
Clear principle ('All Patches Matter, More Patches Better') supported by three lines of evidence: theory, visualization of diverse patch artifacts, and single-patch experiments achieving 90% accuracy
Effective visualizations, particularly Figure 4's TDE heatmaps clearly illustrating the problem and solution's impact, making the work accessible and reproducible
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Random Patch Replacement is straightforward data augmentation (masking and replacement), and Patch-wise Contrastive Learning applies standard margin-based contrastive learning to patches. Neither component is novel individually, and synergistic benefits are not deeply analyzed

Causal inference gaps: While TDE shows which patches have low impact on logits, it doesn't definitively prove patches are 'underutilized'—low TDE could indicate either non-utilization or genuinely weak discriminative signals. Circular reasoning: observing more-patch methods generalize better, then proposing more-patch learning, then showing it generalizes better doesn't establish causality

Incomplete methodological justification: Replacement ratio r, margin parameter α, patch partitioning size m, and contrastive loss choice (why margin-based vs. NT-Xent?) are never ablated or explained. Critical detail omitted: how many reconstructed images added? From which diffusion model? This could significantly confound results

Computational overhead unaddressed: Paper acknowledges 30GB GPU memory requirement but provides no analysis of training time, inference latency, or FLOPs compared to baselines. PCL requires O(n²) patch pair comparisons; cost-benefit tradeoff not quantified

Limited scope: Restricted to fully AI-generated images (excludes composite/local fakes); all images center-cropped to 224×224 without resolution scaling analysis; assumes uniform artifact distribution across diverse architectures

Missing theoretical justification: Why does uniform patch utilization improve generalization? Connection only empirically demonstrated. No analysis of what features each patch learns, visualization of learned representations, or explanation of PCL's specific effectiveness

Experimental fairness concerns: Unclear whether baselines received equivalent computational resources and training enhancements (reconstructed images, data augmentation). Chameleon accuracy (72%) remains modest in absolute terms despite relative improvement

Ablation limitations: Table 4 only tests full component combination; missing ablations on critical hyperparameters (r ∈ [0,1], α, patch size m). Technical detail (Equation 1): masking by zeroing is crude; why not use real patch statistics?

strengths: Clear articulation of well-motivated principles (All Patches Matter, More Patches Better) with multi-faceted empirical validation
Rigorous problem analysis using causal inference (TDE) to quantify Few-Patch Bias across multiple baselines
Strong and comprehensive experimental results across three major datasets (GenImage, DRCT, Chameleon) with significantly lower standard deviation than baselines
Thorough robustness evaluation including JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, and random masking experiments
Well-designed ablation study confirming the necessity and complementarity of both RPR and PCL components
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Random Patch Replacement is standard data augmentation (similar to mixup/cutout); Patch-wise Contrastive Learning is straightforward application of margin-based contrastive loss. Individual components are not novel.

Weak theoretical justification for why the approach works: No explanation of why uniform patch utilization improves cross-generator generalization. The connection between uniform TDE distribution and better generalization is empirically observed but not principled.

TDE analysis has methodological limitations: Masking patches to zero is crude (real attention redistributes); no justification for why TDE variance is the right metric; causality claims are unsupported

Experimental fairness concerns: Method uses stronger CLIP/DINOv2 backbones while many baselines use ResNet-50; reconstructed diffusion images added to training set but not clearly ablated; Chameleon evaluation uses entire GenImage while some baselines may not
Incomplete sensitivity analysis: Missing ablations on replacement ratio r, distance threshold α, loss weight λ, and patch size choices; computational overhead not quantified

Limited generalization scope: Focuses explicitly on fully AI-generated images; only diffusion/GAN models tested; Chameleon still limited despite being called 'challenging'; unknown applicability to future architectures
Statistical rigor concerns: No significance testing despite reporting standard deviations; some improvements are modest (97.2% vs 95.8%); improvement margins overlap with noise in some cases
Unclear component interactions: Ablation shows both help but doesn't characterize synergy; unclear whether PCL is necessary given RPR already addresses the identified problem
Reproducibility: Requires 30 GB GPU memory; some implementation details deferred to appendix; code availability not mentioned; baseline reimplementations may not be faithful

Overclaimed theoretical insights: 'All Patches Matter' is somewhat tautological; 'More Patches Better' presented as universal without qualification; claims about contrastive learning ensuring 'consistent discriminative capability' lack justification

strengths: Clear and well-motivated principles ('All Patches Matter, More Patches Better') that are specific to AIGI detection and distinguish it from conventional classification tasks
Thorough and insightful counterfactual analysis using TDE to demonstrate few-patch bias in existing detectors, with compelling visualizations of attention maps and patch importance distributions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (GenImage, DRCT, Chameleon) and two evaluation settings, with strong empirical results, particularly impressive 70% accuracy on Chameleon vs. ~55% for prior SOTA
Extensive robustness studies demonstrating resilience to image corruptions, patch masking, and other perturbations, showing only 5% recall decline under extreme conditions
Simple and practical methodology (RPR and PCL) that can be readily applied to existing architectures without major modifications
Proper ablation studies (Table 4) showing the contribution of each component
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations that clearly communicate the problem and solution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Random Patch Replacement is standard augmentation, and patch-wise contrastive learning uses well-established margin-based loss from 2006; the contribution is primarily combining existing techniques rather than methodological innovation

Theoretical gaps in core motivation: (1) 'All Patches Matter' assumes uniform artifact distribution across patches and generators without rigorous justification; (2) connection between uniform TDE distribution and generalization is observed only on 3 methods with no statistical or theoretical proof; (3) single-patch experiment (90% accuracy) tested only on SDv1.4 subset

Critical fairness concern in experimental setup: paper mentions adding 'reconstructed images with diffusion process' to training (similar to DRCT) but does not clearly specify if all baseline methods received identical data augmentation, potentially unfairly advantaging PPL in Tables 1-3

Methodological concern with TDE analysis: masking patches to zero is not equivalent to removing patch information, as zero values can be informative; no comparison with alternative masking strategies or direct importance measures

Reproducibility issues: missing key hyperparameters (replacement ratio r, margin α, weight λ), no multiple runs reported, no code availability mentioned, ablation study limited to single backbone (CLIP) and dataset

Limited scope of failure analysis: no discussion of when 'all patches matter' assumption fails, which generative models the method struggles with, or scenarios where artifacts are non-uniformly distributed
Inconsistent experimental validation: ablation study (Table 4) conducted on only one backbone and dataset; unclear if findings generalize to DINOv2 backbone and other datasets used in main results

strengths: Well-motivated diagnosis of Few-Patch Bias with novel quantitative analysis using Controlled Direct Effect (CDE) from causal inference

Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple diverse datasets (GenImage, DRCT-2M, AIGCDetectionBenchmark, UniversalFakeDetect, Chameleon) with impressive generalization to unseen generators
Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablation studies on hyperparameters, module contributions, and robustness under image corruptions
Impressive cross-generator generalization: training on diffusion-generated images achieves strong performance on GAN-generated images, even surpassing baselines trained on GAN data
Excellent visualization and interpretability through CDE heatmaps, attention maps, and GradCAM, effectively demonstrating the method's effectiveness
Well-specified implementation details with justified architectural choices; reproducibility well-supported
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (RPR via diffusion reconstruction, PCL via contrastive learning) are relatively standard techniques; contribution primarily lies in their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Method specificity and computational constraints: heavy reliance on SDv1.4 diffusion reconstruction with specific hyperparameters (s=0.25, 50 steps); PCL adds 18% memory overhead and 33% training time per epoch

Insufficient theoretical justification for why uniform patch utilization improves cross-generator generalization; causal link between Few-Patch Bias and poor generalization is asserted but not rigorously established
Limited mechanistic analysis: unclear why PCL specifically helps or how diffusion-to-GAN generalization works; 'Lazy Learner' concept lacks formal theoretical grounding

Experimental concerns: Table 3 compares PPL (trained on GenImage SDv1.4) against baselines trained on different data (ProGAN), acknowledged as unfair; near-ceiling effects on DRCT-2M (98-99%+ accuracy) limit interpretability of improvements

Incomplete comparative analysis: limited exploration of alternative patch-balancing strategies beyond dropout; only two contrastive losses tested; no comparison with other regularization approaches that could address Few-Patch Bias
Statistical rigor gaps: standard deviations reported only across models rather than across multiple runs with different random seeds; confidence intervals missing for main results

Presentation could be more concise: concepts repeated across sections; Algorithm 1 for PCL is straightforward and doesn't require full algorithm box; connection between RPR and PCL could be clearer upfront

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with strong empirical evidence of few-patch bias through attention visualizations, patch occlusion experiments, and CDE quantitative analysis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5+ datasets with consistent improvements and state-of-the-art results (97.2% mAcc on GenImage)
Thorough ablation studies investigating hyperparameters, component contributions, patch sizes, and alternative designs (Figures 7-8, Tables 6-9)
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and logical structure; detailed appendix with additional analyses
Addresses a practically important problem for AIGI detection with a pragmatic solution that achieves good empirical results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RPR is standard diffusion-based augmentation; PCL is straightforward application of margin-based contrastive learning to patches. The contribution is primarily in combining existing techniques, which feels incremental for a top-tier venue

Shallow theoretical understanding: The connection between the identified few-patch bias problem and the proposed solution is indirect. Why does forcing uniform patch utilization via contrastive learning specifically address lazy learning? Why not simpler alternatives?

Misapplication of causal inference: CDE measures patch contribution to logit differences, not causality. The paper conflates 'underutilized patches' with 'lazy learner effect' without rigorously establishing the mechanism or ruling out alternatives

Questionable design choices: Ablations (Table 9) show random patch dropout also works; this suggests diffusion reconstruction may not be mechanistically necessary. Hyperparameters (s=0.25, λ=0.3) appear empirically chosen without principled justification

Evaluation fairness concerns: Table 3 compares methods trained on different data (baselines on ProGAN, PPL on SDv1.4), undermining claims about GAN generalization. This is acknowledged but not addressed
Suspiciously low variance: Table 2 reports 0.1% std for PPL on DRCT-2M; lacks statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Oversimplified PCL formulation: Binary synthetic/real patch labels ignore artifact variation within each category. Contrastive loss may be overly coarse-grained for this problem

Limited mechanistic insight: Paper doesn't explain which previously-neglected patches are now being utilized, how their representations change, or why contrastive learning is specifically necessary vs. other uniformity constraints

strengths: Clear identification and quantification of 'Few-Patch Bias' in existing AIGI detectors through multiple evidence sources (attention maps, CDE analysis, patch masking)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 major datasets with strong and consistent empirical results (97.2% mAcc on GenImage, 99.50% on DRCT-2M)
Well-motivated principles ('All Patches Matter, More Patches Better') grounded in the properties of generative models
Thorough ablation studies and sensitivity analyses of hyperparameters and design choices
Strong generalization capabilities, including to in-the-wild data (70% on Chameleon vs ~50% for baselines) and cross-model transfer from diffusion to GAN generators
Effective use of interpretability tools (CDE heatmaps, GradCAM) to visualize and understand detector behavior
Practical method applicable to different backbones with clear implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RPR is standard diffusion-based augmentation and PCL is straightforward contrastive learning; the contribution is primarily in their combination rather than fundamentally new techniques

Design choices lack rigorous justification: why diffusion reconstruction over alternatives (minimal comparison beyond patch dropout), arbitrary hyperparameter selection (s=0.25, 50 steps), incomplete rationale for margin-based over InfoNCE loss

CDE analysis limitations: measures only logit difference (simplistic proxy for contribution), lacks theoretical grounding for why uniform CDE uniformity is optimal, no exploration of alternative contribution metrics
Incomplete computational cost analysis: training time for RPR, inference overhead, and cost-benefit tradeoffs not thoroughly discussed despite practical importance
Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars on main results, no significance testing, 'strong generalization' claims overstated (all test generators in standard benchmarks, not truly unseen)
Methodological dependencies: requires SDv1.4 for training, no code release mentioned, dependency on specific diffusion model limits flexibility

Experimental gaps: no failure case analysis, dramatic fake/real accuracy splits on Chameleon not adequately discussed (e.g., Table 5: 17.27/99.01), missing ablations with simple attention regularization baselines
Presentation issues: Figure 1(b) radar chart difficult to interpret, dense organization with many figures that could be condensed or moved to appendix
